text.title: Diary Study Execution and Analysis Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for a diary study already in the field: monitoring compliance while it is still recoverable, separating event time from entry time so backfilled entries cannot contaminate temporal claims, mechanical low-quality criteria, versioned codebooks, a second coder on a sample, and patterns weighted by participants rather than entries.

rule.statement: `compliance_log` MUST be updated at every expected entry window, and two consecutively missed windows MUST trigger a personal contact (message from a named researcher, not another automated reminder) within 24 hours. Check: every flagged gap in the log has a dated remediation action beside it.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, "Diary Methods" (Annual Review of Psychology, 2003) — attrition dynamics

rule.rationale: Diary drop-off is recoverable in the first days and effectively irreversible after. A participant who has been silent for a week does not backfill honestly — they reconstruct — so a compliance check performed at the end of fieldwork can only measure the loss, never prevent it.

rule.statement: Every entry MUST carry both the time the event occurred and the time the entry was submitted. Entries written more than 24 hours after the event MUST be marked `retrospective` and excluded from `temporal_patterns`, though they may still be coded for content.

rationale.source: Stone, Shiffman, Schwartz, Broderick & Hufford, instrumented paper-diary compliance study (BMJ, 2002)

rule.rationale: Instrumenting paper diary binders showed reported compliance around 90% against actual compliance around 11% — participants hoarded entries and filled several at once before hand-in. Backfilled timings telescope toward the present and toward round hours, so mixing them in destroys precisely the time-of-day structure the study was run to find.

rule.statement: `low_quality_entries` MUST be produced by criteria written before analysis and applied mechanically — for example: free-text under N words with no event reference; text duplicating the previous entry verbatim; all fields submitted within seconds of the reminder with identical values to the last submission. Each entry MUST carry a reason and one of a fixed action set (probe at exit, exclude, keep-with-flag).
rule.rationale: Judged-by-feel exclusion is unauditable, and the analyst is the person with a forming story: the entries that get called low quality drift toward the entries that disagree with it. A pre-written criterion makes the exclusion rate itself reportable data about the instrument.

rule.statement: `codebook` MUST give each code a definition and a real example entry, and MUST be versioned. When a new code is added mid-pass, all previously coded entries MUST be re-screened against it, or the artefact MUST state explicitly which entry range never had the chance to receive that code.

rationale.source: Qualitative coding practice; Krippendorff, Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology

rule.rationale: A code invented at entry 200 was unavailable to entries 1-199, so its frequency profile encodes coding order rather than participant behaviour. The distortion is invisible in the output: the code appears to emerge later in the study, which reads as a temporal finding.

rule.statement: A second coder MUST independently code a random 10-20% sample of entries; agreement MUST be computed and reported, and disagreements MUST be resolved by amending the code definition, not by discussion until one coder yields. Krippendorff's alpha at or above .80 supports firm conclusions; .667-.80 supports tentative ones only.

rationale.source: Krippendorff, Content Analysis — reliability thresholds for alpha

rule.rationale: Single-coder coding drifts: the same sentence receives different codes in week one and week three, and the coder cannot detect it from inside. The sample check is the only evidence that the codebook describes the data rather than the coder, and the alpha thresholds are what makes "we agreed" falsifiable.

rule.statement: Each `temporal_patterns` item MUST state the number of distinct participants supporting it, the number of entries, and the time window it holds over. A pattern supported by a single participant MUST be labelled a case. Entry counts alone MUST NOT be reported as prevalence.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli (2003) — nested structure of diary data (entries within persons)

rule.rationale: Diary corpora are dominated by two or three prolific writers who can contribute several times the median entry count. An unweighted entry tally therefore reads as consensus while describing one enthusiastic participant, and the nesting of entries within people is exactly what the analysis must not ignore.

rule.statement: Skip when (a) fieldwork has already closed and no compliance intervention is possible — go straight to coding and report the compliance rate as a limitation; (b) fewer participants cleared the compliance threshold than the study's own minimum, in which case report the failed study rather than coding the survivors; (c) entries were collected without event timestamps, so no temporal claim is supportable; (d) the corpus is small enough (tens of entries, one or two participants) that coding machinery adds ceremony over simply reading and quoting it.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions for longitudinal self-report analysis

rule.rationale: Coding a corpus that failed its own compliance threshold manufactures a defensible-looking analysis on top of a biased sample; the codebook and the alpha score then lend credibility that the underlying data does not have.
